page2_img_1.png.title: Side-by-side JavaScript and TypeScript examples showing added TypeScript annotations
page2_img_1.png.description: A two-panel code snippet: the left panel is un-annotated JavaScript for a function addStyleSheet(ownerDocument, cssText) and the right panel is the TypeScript equivalent with explicit types. The TypeScript version adds annotations such as ownerDocument: Document, cssText: string, var p: HTMLElement, var parent: HTMLElement, and an annotated p.innerHTML : string, while the function’s return is marked as any. The juxtaposition highlights which types are obvious from usage (createElement implies HTMLElement) versus those that require explicit annotation (cssText as string) and serves as an example of the aligned JS/TS pairs used to train DeepTyper.

page7_img_1.png.title: Web UI showing source code and DeepTyper type suggestions with confidence scores
page7_img_1.png.description: Screenshot of the DeepTyper web interface displaying a side-by-side view: a 'Source' panel on the left with the original JavaScript function addStyleSheet(ownerDocument, cssText) and its body (createElement, getElementsByTagName, innerHTML, insertBefore), and a 'Target' panel on the right where inferred TypeScript annotations are shown. A popup over the Target panel lists the model's ranked type suggestions (with probabilities) for the selected identifier: HTMLElement (65.81%), Element (10.97%), HTMLDivElement (8.67%), Document (5.15%), and complex (0.65%). The UI includes a confidence slider/header labeled “Minimum Confidence: 50%” (with a colored bar) and an “Infer Types!” button, indicating the tool both proposes top-k type candidates and lets the user control a confidence threshold for presenting suggestions.

page9_img_table_1.png.title: Correctness breakdown: JSNice vs DeepTyper vs Hybrid
page9_img_table_1.png.description: Table shows a per-annotation outcome comparison (correct, partial, incorrect, unsure) for JSNice, DeepTyper at three confidence thresholds (≥0%, ≥50%, ≥90%), and a Hybrid approach, evaluated on 30 JavaScript functions (167 annotations). JSNice achieves 51.9% correct, 1.9% partial, 0.9% incorrect and is unsure 45.4% of the time. DeepTyper at no confidence threshold is more aggressive (55.6% correct) but makes more incorrect predictions (6.5%) with 35.2% unsure; raising the threshold to ≥50% reduces incorrects to 2.8% (51.9% correct, 44.4% unsure) and to ≥90% eliminates incorrects entirely (35.2% correct, 64.8% unsure). The Hybrid (combining JSNice and DeepTyper) yields the highest correct rates (71.3% correct at ≥0% threshold) while substantially lowering the unsure rate (20.4%), and maintains good trade-offs at higher confidence thresholds (e.g., 64.8% correct and 0.9% incorrect at ≥90%).

page5_img_table_1.png.title: Dataset split: projects, files, and tokens (Train / Held-out / Test)
page5_img_table_1.png.description: A three-row table reporting the dataset used to train and evaluate DeepTyper, broken down by split: Train (620 projects, 49,850 files, 17,955,121 tokens), Held-out (78 projects, 7,854 files, 3,918,175 tokens), and Test (78 projects, 4,650 files, 1,884,385 tokens). These rows sum to 776 projects and 62,354 files (23,757,681 tokens) consistent with the paper’s 80%/10%/10% split by project: the training split contains roughly 80% of projects and files and about 75.6% of tokens, while each held-out and test split consist of 78 projects (~10% each) with held-out containing ~16.5% of tokens and test ~7.9% of tokens. This table quantifies the scale of code (millions of tokens) available for model training and evaluation.

page5_img_diagram_1.png.title: Experimental pipeline: data collection, DeepTyper training, and evaluation
page5_img_diagram_1.png.description: A three-phase pipeline diagram linking GitHub, the TypeScript compiler, the Deep Learner, and evaluation tools. Blue (dashed) arrows show data collection: the GitHub API feeds projects into the TypeScript compiler to produce aligned Tokens and Types. Green (solid) arrows indicate training: the Deep Learner consumes Tokens and learns from the aligned Types (bidirectional arrow between Deep Learner and Types). Yellow (dashed) arrows show deployment/evaluation: the learned model and types are exposed via a Web API and combined with CheckJS for hybrid type-suggestion and evaluation; the circled numbers 1, 2, and 3 label the stages (data gathering, learning, evaluation) described in the paper.

page4_img_1.png.title: Neural architecture for token-to-type prediction with consistency layer
page4_img_1.png.description: Diagram of DeepTyper’s sequence‑tagging network that maps a token sequence (bottom) to predicted type vectors (top). Tokens are embedded (300‑dim) and passed through two stacked bidirectional GRU layers (each 650‑dim); the example input shows the token stream "var x = 0 ; var y = x ;" with the two occurrences of x highlighted in orange and y in blue. A consistency module (orange arrows into a central + node) averages the biGRU representations of all occurrences of the same identifier and feeds that signal back into the second biGRU so the model leans toward a single, consistent type across uses. The final projection layer maps each token representation to a vocabulary-sized type vector (illustrated as circles: grey '-' for non-identifier/no-type and green 'num' for number), which is interpreted as a probability distribution over types for each token.

page8_img_table_1.png.title: Hybrid accuracy, hits and misses at varying DeepTyper confidence thresholds
page8_img_table_1.png.description: The table compares three approaches: CJ (TypeScript+CheckJS) with a constant top-1 accuracy of 10.5%, DT (DeepTyper) with a constant top-1 accuracy of 56.9%, and a Hybrid that uses DeepTyper suggestions when CheckJS yields any or (in a second block) when DeepTyper may override all CheckJS judgments. Rows show results for two modes—‘any’ (DeepTyper may only replace anys) and ‘all’—at DT confidence thresholds 90%, 99%, and 99.9%. For the ‘any’ setting, Hybrid accuracy declines from 37.6% (90%) to 20.6% (99%) to 12.2% (99.9%), while Hits (correctly converting anys to concrete types) fall from 27.1% → 10.2% → 1.80% and Misses (incorrect replacements) fall from 1.22% → 0.07% → 0.00%. The ‘all’ setting shows similar behavior (Hybrid accuracy 38.5%/21.1%/12.3%; Hits 28.2%/10.7%/1.85%; Misses 1.41%/0.09%/0.00%), illustrating that raising the DeepTyper confidence threshold reduces both added correct annotations and added errors (trading recall for higher precision).

page8_img_1.png.title: DeepTyper precision–recall trade-off across confidence thresholds
page8_img_1.png.description: A precision versus recall curve for DeepTyper’s top-type suggestion when varying the model confidence threshold. The curve slopes downward: requiring higher confidence raises precision but reduces recall — for example, using a 90% confidence cutoff yields roughly 80% precision at about 50% recall, while a 99% cutoff gives over 95% precision at roughly 15% recall (very high-confidence cutoffs approach ≈99% precision but with near-zero recall). The figure illustrates the practical trade-off the authors exploit to present only very-precise type suggestions to developers (so fewer, high-quality annotations can be offered automatically).
